ann_78.original: Customer-service calls raise the predicted churn risk steeply once a customer has made several of them while daytime use is low or average; for heavy daytime users the calls make little difference until the count is high. Self-probe (the typical customer, with daytime minutes and day charge set together): at 120 daytime minutes ($20.40 day charge) the predicted risk is 1% with 0 calls, 16% with 3 and 70% with 4; at 180 minutes ($30.60) it is 3% with 2 calls, 13% with 4 and 57% with 5; at 240 minutes ($40.80) it is 15% with 0 calls, still 15% with 6 and 38% with 7. So the number of calls at which risk takes off moves up as the day charge rises. In the training data, the 156 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge under $30 churned at 75.6% (mean predicted risk 65.5%), and through this part their score is on average 5.30 above the part's training average; the 162 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge of $30 or more churned at 25.3%, and for them the part adds 0.20 on average. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.759. Mechanism: two hinged units (node 104 and node 7506) open as calls rise and close as the day charge rises; each feeds the score directly and through a follower unit (7664 and 9029). Small extras: New Hampshire and Connecticut indicators enter node 104, and a Florida-specific unit (node 2039) opens on 3 training rows, so it is fitted to those rows. The formula evidence rounds coefficients to three significant figures (off by up to 0.016 on the part's output over the training rows).
ann_78.proposed: More calls to customer service raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves, slowly at first, then faster, mainly when the daytime charge is low: for a typical customer with total daytime charge at or below 30.69 US dollars, from about 1% at 0 calls to about 9% at 3 calls, while with a higher charge it stays at about 6% over that range and rises beyond it. A higher daytime charge lowers the chance through this part in an uneven way, mostly below about 25.31 US dollars (between 23.90 US dollars and 32.87 US dollars for different customers).

ann_79.original: More daytime minutes raise the predicted churn risk, and the rise steepens for heavy daytime users when a second unit (node 6238) opens. Through its own edge into this part, daytime minutes add 1.10 to the score per standard deviation; the hinge adds 1.73 times its value on top. Self-probe (the typical customer, sweeping daytime minutes with the day charge held at its typical value so that the service-call part stays fixed): predicted risk is 1% at 100 minutes, 4% at 200, 22% at 250 and 73% at 300; the hinge is at 0.00 at 200 minutes and 0.13 at 225, so the steeper climb starts between 200 and 225 minutes. In the training data the hinge is open for 1002 of 4000 customers; they churned at 28.4% against 9.4% for the rest, and through this part their score is on average 2.00 above the part's training average. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.772. A New York indicator also enters the hinge, with weight -0.018 against 0.77 for daytime minutes. Together with the service-call part this gives two churn routes on daytime use: heavy daytime users are at risk through this part, light users with many service calls through the other.
ann_79.proposed: More daytime minutes raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical customer, from about 1% at 112 minutes to about 21% at 249 minutes (with the matching daytime charge).

ann_80.original: Customers with longer accounts get a slightly higher predicted churn risk, with a steeper rise for the longest accounts. Account length adds 0.11 to the score per standard deviation through its own edge into this part, and a hinge (node 11575) adds 0.26 times its value once it opens. Self-probe (the typical customer, sweeping account length): predicted risk is 2% at an account length of 25, 3% at 100 and 6% at 225; the hinge is 0.00 at 125 and 0.09 at 150, so it opens between 125 and 150. The hinge is open for 488 of 4000 training customers, who churned at 15.8% against 13.9% for the rest, a weak difference; switching the part off moves the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.899. This is a small adjustment that the observed churn rates barely support.
ann_80.proposed: A longer account raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves a little, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical customer from about 2% at an account length of 48 to about 3% at 152.

ann_81.original: The customer's state shifts the score by a fixed amount per state. Because the state inputs are one-hot indicators, each hidden unit in this part (nodes 4253, 11955, 11236 and 1084, and 2730 with 6958) takes one value for customers of its state and another for everyone else, so the part acts as a per-state lookup table. Self-probe (the typical customer, moved through the 51 states): predicted risk is 2.8% in West Virginia, a state without a term of its own; it rises to 12.0% in California, 10.2% in Washington, 6.8% in Montana, 6.6% in New Jersey and 5.8% in Texas, and falls to 0.6% in Vermont, 1.2% in Alaska and 1.2% in New Hampshire. Maryland's offset comes through a hinge (node 4253) that is on for other states and off for Maryland: its risk is 4.1%. The direction of the offsets follows the training churn rates: the 41 California customers churned at 26.8% and the 72 Washington customers at 29.2%, against 6.2% for the 80 Vermont customers. The sizes are larger than these counts warrant: on the logit scale the model gives Vermont -1.57 where the shrunken empirical estimate is -0.78, California 1.56 against 0.79, and Washington 1.38 against 0.68, so these offsets look partly fitted to small state samples. Units 2730 and 6958 (fed by the Colorado and Indiana indicators) are open on 0 of the 4000 training rows, and node 2730 is 0.00 even for a Colorado customer in the probe, so they are dead and Colorado and Indiana get the baseline. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.893.
ann_81.proposed: The state moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves: for a typical customer about 3% in West Virginia, about 12% in California, about 10% in Washington and about 1% in Vermont.

ann_82.original: An international plan raises the predicted churn risk sharply and a voice-mail plan lowers it; more evening and international minutes raise it and more international calls lower it. These are plain additive terms with no interaction inside the part. Through their own edges into this part, per standard deviation: international plan 0.74, voice-mail plan -0.84, number of voice-mail messages 0.30, evening minutes 0.50, international minutes 0.32 and international calls -0.21; the night-time, day-call and area-code terms are smaller (see the formula evidence). Self-probe (the typical customer): with 150 evening minutes the predicted risk is 2% without and 18% with an international plan; with 250 evening minutes it is 4% and 37%. The score moves from -4.07 to -1.53 at 150 evening minutes and from -3.07 to -0.53 at 250, a step of equal size, as an additive part predicts. For the voice-mail plan the predicted risk is 3% without a plan, below 1% with a plan and no messages and 1% with a plan and 30 messages: the message count gives back part of the plan's reduction. In the training data the 380 customers with an international plan churned at 42.4% against 11.2% for the rest (their mean predicted risk is 43.8%), and the 1061 voice-mail plan holders churned at 7.4% against 16.6%. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.824.
ann_82.proposed: An international plan raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves (for a typical customer from about 3% to about 27%) and a voice-mail plan lowers it (to about 1%); more evening and international minutes raise it steadily and more international calls lower it steadily.

ann_83.original: The model adds the five parts on the logit scale and passes the sum through a sigmoid; three churn routes dominate: many customer-service calls with low or average daytime use, heavy daytime use, and an international plan, with a voice-mail plan, the state and account length as smaller adjustments. The model's training AUC is 0.901; switching one part off lowers it to 0.759 for the service-call part, 0.772 for daytime minutes, 0.824 for plans and usage, 0.893 for the state offsets and 0.899 for account length. Self-probe of the additive combination (the typical customer at 180 daytime minutes and a $30.60 day charge): predicted risk is 3% with 1 service call and no international plan, 13% with 4 calls, 26% with an international plan and 66% with both, so two routes together push the risk well above either alone, as a sum of scores predicts (scores -3.57, -1.87, -1.03 and 0.67). The remaining inputs (most state indicators, two area codes, evening calls and charge, international charge) are not connected to the output. Recombining the parts reproduces the original network: the largest difference over the training rows is 4.4e-16.
ann_83.proposed: The model adds the scores of five parts: calls to customer service weighed against the daytime charge, daytime minutes, the plans and other usage, the state, and the account length. For a typical customer the predicted chance that a customer leaves is about 3%; an international plan raises it to about 27%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to about 1%.

parts.original_hypothesis: The model adds the five parts on the logit scale and passes the sum through a sigmoid; three churn routes dominate: many customer-service calls with low or average daytime use, heavy daytime use, and an international plan, with a voice-mail plan, the state and account length as smaller adjustments. The model's training AUC is 0.901; switching one part off lowers it to 0.759 for the service-call part, 0.772 for daytime minutes, 0.824 for plans and usage, 0.893 for the state offsets and 0.899 for account length. Self-probe of the additive combination (the typical customer at 180 daytime minutes and a $30.60 day charge): predicted risk is 3% with 1 service call and no international plan, 13% with 4 calls, 26% with an international plan and 66% with both, so two routes together push the risk well above either alone, as a sum of scores predicts (scores -3.57, -1.87, -1.03 and 0.67). The remaining inputs (most state indicators, two area codes, evening calls and charge, international charge) are not connected to the output. Recombining the parts reproduces the original network: the largest difference over the training rows is 4.4e-16.

parts.name: service_calls_low_day_charge
parts.original_hypothesis: Customer-service calls raise the predicted churn risk steeply once a customer has made several of them while daytime use is low or average; for heavy daytime users the calls make little difference until the count is high. Self-probe (the typical customer, with daytime minutes and day charge set together): at 120 daytime minutes ($20.40 day charge) the predicted risk is 1% with 0 calls, 16% with 3 and 70% with 4; at 180 minutes ($30.60) it is 3% with 2 calls, 13% with 4 and 57% with 5; at 240 minutes ($40.80) it is 15% with 0 calls, still 15% with 6 and 38% with 7. So the number of calls at which risk takes off moves up as the day charge rises. In the training data, the 156 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge under $30 churned at 75.6% (mean predicted risk 65.5%), and through this part their score is on average 5.30 above the part's training average; the 162 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge of $30 or more churned at 25.3%, and for them the part adds 0.20 on average. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.759. Mechanism: two hinged units (node 104 and node 7506) open as calls rise and close as the day charge rises; each feeds the score directly and through a follower unit (7664 and 9029). Small extras: New Hampshire and Connecticut indicators enter node 104, and a Florida-specific unit (node 2039) opens on 3 training rows, so it is fitted to those rows. The formula evidence rounds coefficients to three significant figures (off by up to 0.016 on the part's output over the training rows).

parts.name: daytime_minutes
parts.original_hypothesis: More daytime minutes raise the predicted churn risk, and the rise steepens for heavy daytime users when a second unit (node 6238) opens. Through its own edge into this part, daytime minutes add 1.10 to the score per standard deviation; the hinge adds 1.73 times its value on top. Self-probe (the typical customer, sweeping daytime minutes with the day charge held at its typical value so that the service-call part stays fixed): predicted risk is 1% at 100 minutes, 4% at 200, 22% at 250 and 73% at 300; the hinge is at 0.00 at 200 minutes and 0.13 at 225, so the steeper climb starts between 200 and 225 minutes. In the training data the hinge is open for 1002 of 4000 customers; they churned at 28.4% against 9.4% for the rest, and through this part their score is on average 2.00 above the part's training average. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.772. A New York indicator also enters the hinge, with weight -0.018 against 0.77 for daytime minutes. Together with the service-call part this gives two churn routes on daytime use: heavy daytime users are at risk through this part, light users with many service calls through the other.

parts.name: state_offsets
parts.original_hypothesis: The customer's state shifts the score by a fixed amount per state. Because the state inputs are one-hot indicators, each hidden unit in this part (nodes 4253, 11955, 11236 and 1084, and 2730 with 6958) takes one value for customers of its state and another for everyone else, so the part acts as a per-state lookup table. Self-probe (the typical customer, moved through the 51 states): predicted risk is 2.8% in West Virginia, a state without a term of its own; it rises to 12.0% in California, 10.2% in Washington, 6.8% in Montana, 6.6% in New Jersey and 5.8% in Texas, and falls to 0.6% in Vermont, 1.2% in Alaska and 1.2% in New Hampshire. Maryland's offset comes through a hinge (node 4253) that is on for other states and off for Maryland: its risk is 4.1%. The direction of the offsets follows the training churn rates: the 41 California customers churned at 26.8% and the 72 Washington customers at 29.2%, against 6.2% for the 80 Vermont customers. The sizes are larger than these counts warrant: on the logit scale the model gives Vermont -1.57 where the shrunken empirical estimate is -0.78, California 1.56 against 0.79, and Washington 1.38 against 0.68, so these offsets look partly fitted to small state samples. Units 2730 and 6958 (fed by the Colorado and Indiana indicators) are open on 0 of the 4000 training rows, and node 2730 is 0.00 even for a Colorado customer in the probe, so they are dead and Colorado and Indiana get the baseline. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.893.

parts.original_hypothesis: Customers with longer accounts get a slightly higher predicted churn risk, with a steeper rise for the longest accounts. Account length adds 0.11 to the score per standard deviation through its own edge into this part, and a hinge (node 11575) adds 0.26 times its value once it opens. Self-probe (the typical customer, sweeping account length): predicted risk is 2% at an account length of 25, 3% at 100 and 6% at 225; the hinge is 0.00 at 125 and 0.09 at 150, so it opens between 125 and 150. This is a small adjustment that the observed churn rates barely support.

ann_78.text: A higher customer-service calls clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, mainly if total daytime charge is at or below 30.69 US dollars (it also changes for 305 of the 1997 training customers for whom it does not hold) (slowly at first, then faster for patients with total daytime charge at or below 30.69 US dollars): for a typical customer, customer-service calls going from 0 calls to 3 calls moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% to about 9% if total daytime charge is at or below 30.69 US dollars (with total daytime minutes at 144 minutes, as in the data), and from about 6% to about 6% if total daytime charge is above 30.69 US dollars (with total daytime minutes at 216 minutes, as in the data) (above 3 calls it changes for them too: from about 6% to above 99% at 9 calls).

For a typical customer, total daytime charge going from 19.07 US dollars to 42.40 US dollars moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 9% to about 6% if the customer is in New Hampshire, and from about 3% to about 13% if state is something other than New Hampshire, Connecticut, Florida (it moves in a curve that is lowest at about 28.35 US dollars, higher either side for customers in New Hampshire).

Through this part, total daytime charge clearly lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves while it stays below about 25.31 US dollars (between 23.90 and 32.87 US dollars for different customers) (for 1779 of the 4000 training customers it already changes above that): for a typical such customer, going from 15.49 US dollars to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 14% to about 3%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

Through this part, the model treats a higher total daytime charge as clearly lowering the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from about 9% at 19.07 US dollars to about 3% at 42.40 US dollars (with total daytime minutes at 236 minutes, as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: customer-service calls past about 4 calls raises it in an uneven way; a higher customer-service calls raises it in an uneven way; customer-service calls depending on state raises it in an uneven way; New Hampshire (rather than any other state) raises it; Connecticut (rather than any other state) raises it; Florida (rather than any other state) lowers it (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 8 training customers (of them, patients already past their fold).
